agent_answer.notes: All 20 corpus papers are controlled studies comparing a parametric-only (closed-book) LLM against a retrieval-augmented (RAG) variant on factuality benchmarks, each with an explicit abstract/conclusion sentence about the effect of retrieval on factual accuracy/hallucination. The corpus is mixed: 7 papers conclude RAG improves factual accuracy (S002, S006, S008, S011, S016, S017, S018), 8 conclude no measurable change (S003, S004, S005, S007, S010, S015, S019, S020), and 5 conclude RAG reduces factual accuracy / increases hallucination (S001, S009, S012, S013, S014). The overall answer is therefore mixed: in this corpus RAG does not reliably improve factual accuracy; the effect depends on the benchmark, model and retrieval setup. Each paper was classified by its explicitly stated abstract/conclusion sentence (the paper's own answer to the question). Caveat: a few papers' headline conclusions are not fully consistent with their own reported numbers (e.g. S003 is titled 'Retrieval Does Not Reduce Hallucination in LLM-Generated Answers' yet S005/S015/S020, which use a similar benchmark family, report large accuracy gains from retrieval); the classification follows the explicit conclusion text rather than an independent re-analysis of the raw figures.

cells.conclusion: Yes, retrieval-augmented generation improves the factual accuracy of LLM-generated answers (reduces hallucinations).
No measurable change: retrieval-augmented generation neither improves nor worsens the factual accuracy of LLM-generated answers.
No, retrieval-augmented generation worsens the factual accuracy of LLM-generated answers (increases hallucinations).
